analysis.title: Investor Positioning and Flows - The Spring Is Coiled Again: Upgrading Tech Back To Overweight
key_insights: DB upgrades Tech (mega-cap growth and Tech, 'MCG & Tech') tactically back to overweight from neutral, three weeks after the Oct 9 downgrade. Tech underperformed sharply since, reaching the bottom of its decade-long relative trend channel, and positioning has dropped sharply.
MCG & Tech has underperformed the rest of the S&P 500 by over 16pp in the last three weeks. It fell 11% while the rest of the S&P 500 rose almost 6%.
The relative performance level has produced a V-turn up 5 times in the last 2 1/2 years. DB notes it can go lower around large exogenous shocks, as it did around Liberation Day and the Iran War.
On average, past rotations into Tech saw Tech rise 32% and outperform the rest of the S&P 500 by 30pp. The S&P 500 rose 16% on average over 3 months in those rotations.

Tech positioning fell from clearly elevated levels three weeks ago to neutral (40th percentile). It is now in line with roughly 10% earnings growth, versus about 47% in Q3 and the 36% consensus expects by the end of next year. DB reads positioning as pricing in significant AI-demand risk and post-midterm regulation and scrutiny risk.

Large-cap equity positioning is modestly overweight (66th percentile), but discretionary investors are neutral (48th percentile in the text, 21st percentile in Figure 13 for discretionary vs 79th for systematic). Discretionary positioning is consistent with mid-single-digit earnings growth.

Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth is on track for 31% y/y. Tech and Energy account for 3/4 of it. Growth excluding Tech and Energy is 12% and the median S&P 500 company is growing 14.4%, both around 2-decade highs outside of recession rebounds.
Positioning in sectors outside of Tech is very low (6th percentile) and small-cap positioning is low (22nd percentile), leaving room to catch up with earnings growth.

On post-midterm policy risk, DB argues a lot is already priced in. Before the 2024 election, large-cap positioning was at similar levels to now but in line with earnings growth, not well below it as now.

Oil is priced for significant supply disruption. WTI at $102.0 is 65% above DB's medium-term fair value of $61.8 (a model based on global growth and the US dollar), close to the premium at the peak in the first month of the Iran war. Near-month Brent is more than 15% above the 6th-month contract, similar to prior large supply disruptions.

Systematic positioning is high: consolidated systematic percentile 79%, vol-control equity allocation 77th percentile, risk-parity equity weight 84th percentile (US 88%), and CTA equity exposure 58th percentile (SPX 82%, NDX 55%, RTY 29%).

CTA bond allocation is at the 10th percentile. CTA FX positioning is short or low in several currencies (GBP 0th, NZD 3rd, CAD 6th, EUR 8th, CHF 9th percentile), and CTA oil exposure is at the 79th percentile.
Sentiment: AAII bearish sentiment is at the 84th percentile since 1987, neutral at the 10th, bullish at the 52nd, and bull-minus-bear spread at the 29th percentile.

Options: net call volume is at the 86th percentile since 2010 and the equity call/put ratio at the 57th percentile. Equity L/S hedge fund beta to the S&P 500 is at the 89th percentile on both 1m and 3m measures.
Sector positioning percentiles: Energy 80%, Healthcare 52%, Industrial cyclicals 35%, Real estate 28%, Financials 23%, Consumer cyclicals 17%, Materials 16%, Consumer staples 15%, Utilities 2%.
DB S&P 500 2026 target is 8000, with 2026 EPS of $358 and 2027 EPS of $420.

sector_views.rationale: Tactical upgrade from neutral: relative performance is at the bottom of its trend channel, positioning has fallen to neutral and is now in line with a sharp earnings deceleration, and past rotations into Tech were large.
Positioning outside Tech is at the 6th percentile while growth ex-Tech and Energy is 12%, which DB says leaves room to catch up. DB does not give a formal rating.

earnings_insights: Q3 2026 S&P 500 blended EPS growth is on track for 31% y/y. Blended assumes reporting companies beat at the current beat rate. Tech and Energy account for 3/4 of it.
Q3 growth ex-Tech and Energy is 12% y/y, and the median S&P 500 company is growing 14.4% y/y. Both are around 2-decade highs outside of recession rebounds.
Tech earnings growth was about 47% in Q3 (per DB). Consensus expects 36% by the end of next year. DB says Tech positioning is consistent with roughly 10% growth.
DB S&P 500 EPS forecasts are $358 for 2026 and $420 for 2027.

trade_ideas.description: Tactical overweight Tech (mega-cap growth and Tech) relative to the rest of the S&P 500
trade_ideas.rationale: Relative performance is at the bottom of its trend channel, positioning has fallen to neutral and matches a sharp earnings deceleration, and past rotations into Tech returned an average 32%.
trade_ideas.risk: Tech can fall further around large exogenous shocks, as it did around Liberation Day and the Iran War. Post-midterm Tech regulation and renewed geopolitical escalation are named as risks.

risk_factors: Renewed geopolitical escalation, with oil already priced for significant supply disruption.
AI-demand risk and a sharp deceleration in Tech earnings growth.
Large exogenous shocks can push Tech relative performance below the bottom of its trend channel.
charts_described: Figure 1: MCG & Tech ratio to the rest of the S&P 500 has gone from the top to the bottom of its long-run trend channel in three weeks. Trend growth since 2016 is 14.2% annualized, with a band of +/-10%.

Figure 2 table: the last rotation into Tech (Jul 29 to Oct 7, 2026, 51 trading days) saw MCG & Tech +16.9% and the S&P 500 +6.6%. The latest rotation away (Oct 7 to Oct 30, 2026, 18 trading days) saw MCG & Tech -10.7% and the S&P 500 -2.8%. Median rotation into Tech: MCG & Tech +31.8%, S&P 500 +15.7%.
Figure: WTI at $102.0 vs fitted fair value of $61.8, a 65.0% deviation, from a regression on the dollar and global manufacturing PMI (R-squared 84%, sample Feb 2000 to Dec 2013).
Figure 105/124: bond futures net positioning as of Oct 20 is short across maturities: SOFR -18.6%, 2y -18.9%, 5y -16.0%, 10y -13.0%, 30y -3.8%, Ultra T-bond -15.9% of open interest.
vol_and_positioning: MCG & Tech positioning is at the 40th percentile, down sharply from elevated levels three weeks ago.
Consolidated equity positioning is at the 44th percentile. Discretionary is at the 21st percentile and systematic at the 79th (Figure 13).
Vol-control equity allocation is at the 77th percentile, risk-parity equity weight at the 84th, CTA equity exposure at the 58th.
Single-stock net call volume is high: total net call volume is at the 86th percentile since 2010.
Equity L/S hedge fund beta to the S&P 500 is at the 89th percentile (1m and 3m rolling).
Large-cap Energy positioning is at the 80th percentile, Utilities at the 2nd.
Futures data as of Oct 20: bond futures net positioning is short in all maturities (SOFR -18.6%, 2y -18.9%, 5y -16.0%, 10y -13.0%, 30y -3.8%, Ultra -15.9% of open interest).
Short interest data as of Oct 15; no headline figure is cited in the text.
geopolitical: Renewed geopolitical escalation risk, with the Iran war referenced as the source of the earlier oil premium peak.
Potential regulation targeting Tech after the US mid-term elections next week.

tension_points.bull_case: Tech relative performance is at the bottom of its trend channel, positioning has fallen to neutral and matches roughly 10% earnings growth, and past rotations into Tech returned an average 32%. The S&P 500 also rallied hard in those rotations.
tension_points.bear_case: Post-midterm regulation of Tech, renewed geopolitical escalation and AI-demand risk could push Tech lower, as large exogenous shocks did around Liberation Day and the Iran War.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Large exogenous shocks that push Tech relative performance below the bottom of its trend channel, as around Liberation Day and the Iran War. The report names no specific level.
